speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Since 2012, the existing GST Voucher scheme has been funded from the GST Voucher Fund.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Under this scheme, lower and middle income households receive annual cash payouts, MediSave top-ups, and utilities rebates, or "U-Save" to offset the GST that they pay on their daily expenses.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: In his Budget 2020 Speech, Deputy Prime Minister Heng Swee Keat announced that the Government will introduce an Assurance Package for GST.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The Assurance Package will help Singaporeans cushion the impact of the GST rate increase to 9%.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Deputy Prime Minister Heng Swee Keat has explained why this is necessary to raise recurrent revenues to meet recurrent spending, particularly for healthcare.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Having said that, the weight of our assistance in the GST Voucher Fund will still go toward lower income Singaporeans who will continue to receive more support.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Given the expanded purposes of the Fund, we have also added a new section 8A to safeguard against legal action being inappropriately taken against the GST Voucher Fund, which basically is for general welfare.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The Government will then be able to use the GST Voucher Fund for measures in the transitional package to cushion the GST increase for all Singaporeans, when the GST increase takes effect.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: I want to reiterate that while we are broadening the assistance under the Assurance Package, we will continue to provide more support to lower income Singaporeans during the transition, and over and above this, we will continue to enhance the existing permanent GST Voucher scheme, to provide continued support to lower and middle income households.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Compared to the current provision which targets the identified beneficiaries themselves, the grants-in-aid extend the reach of the Fund to help with the expenses that may be incurred by one person for the benefit of another beneficiary, such as by a family member of an elderly.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: My residents, especially those who are care-givers of their elderly parents welcome this move.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Presently, the Home Caregiving Grant provides $200 monthly cash payouts to care-givers to defray care-giving expenses, such as to be used to partially offset the wages of a foreign domestic worker (FDW) or eldercare fees.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The grants-in-aid will be a much-welcomed supplement as there are quite a number of care-giving expenses, including assistive devices and consumable home healthcare items.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: While the Seniors' Mobility and Enabling Fund provides subsidies to help cover some of these costs, financial assistance to offset the impact of GST on these items will provide added relief.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: (In Mandarin):   The grant-in-aid will be a much-welcomed supplement as there are a number of care-giving expenses, including those assistive devices and consumable home healthcare items.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: While the Seniors' Mobility and Enabling Fund provides subsidies to help some of these costs, financial assistance to offset the impact of GST on these items will provide added relief.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: While the tax itself is straightforward, the policy of using GST Vouchers to correct the impact of the tax on low-income Singaporeans is perhaps less clear at times.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Before I discuss today's proposed amendment to the GST Voucher Fund, I think it useful to outline why the GST Voucher Scheme is crucial to address persistent criticisms of the GST.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Many critics argue that the GST is a regressive tax, that it places a greater burden on lower income Singaporeans and this leads to suggestions that the GST should be waived on necessities, replaced with a tax on luxury goods, or replaced by more progressive income taxes.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: These ideas while well-meaning are likely to be inefficient, compared to our practice of simply granting GST Vouchers to households.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: For example, differentiating between necessities and luxury goods is not straightforward.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: A number of US states exempt groceries from sales tax, but not take-away food.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: This can lead to the perverse result that lobsters are exempt from sales tax but fast food is fully taxed.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: So simply returning the GST paid to lower income households through GST Vouchers is much easier.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Progressive income taxes should be an integral component of any fair taxation system but some critics also present a false choice between raising income taxes and GST.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Income taxes do not cover short-term visitors to Singapore but GST does.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Our present income tax system does not cover most sources of non-wage income to individuals, so GST does help to ensure people pay some taxes out of capital income, windfalls, capital gains, and so on.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: There are reasonable concerns, for example, Ms Pereira raised that retirees are burdened by paying GST.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: But again, returning the GST paid to low-income retirees through GST Vouchers is much easier, while high-income retirees undoubtedly benefit overall from the lack of capital taxes in Singapore.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The permanent GST Voucher Scheme, backed by the GST Voucher Fund, is an ideal solution to the problem of regressivity.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: If it is well designed, it can eliminate most or all of the burden of GST on low-income Singaporeans.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: As GST increases the cash price of purchasing goods and services, it is simplest if cash is just returned to lower income households, so that they end up paying little or no net GST.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Simplicity is also a virtue when it comes to addressing misunderstandings about the GST.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: If that is the case, then would it be really necessary to move this particular part of the amendment?

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Could then the other relief schemes be funded through other means?

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: I would also suggest that the Government annually assess and publish estimates of the amount of GST paid by individuals and households at different parts of the income distribution.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: These could then be compared to the value of GST Voucher payouts, so the actual incidence of the GST on Singaporeans will be transparent.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: This would also be useful for fine-tuning aspects of the GST Voucher Scheme because changes to savings and expenditure patterns in the population could affect the GST incidence people pay.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: But I still think it would be more useful and illuminating if the Ministry could publish estimates on the effective rates of GST at different parts of the income distribution and how this will be impacted by the proposed increases to the GST rate, with the GST Voucher Scheme in mind.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: The Government recognises that GST is a regressive tax.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: First, why is the policy limited only to Singaporeans when GST hurts all lower income residents?

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Second, why expand the scope of beneficiaries to those who do not need the relief when there are people in our midst who need it but do not get it?

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: They will suffer from the GST hike and are being offered no relief.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: It seems counter-intuitive to give money to individuals who do not need the relief while denying those who do.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: In fact, when we consider migrant workers' centrality to the building of our nation, it seems almost perverse.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Singapore relies on an enormous foreign workforce to sustain the construction, marine, manufacturing and domestic work sectors.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Seventy percent of them were work permit holders.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: That is about 17% of the population and 26% of our resident labour force.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: They most commonly come from India, China, Bangladesh, Indonesia and the Philippines.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Low-wage migrant workers are most commonly employed in construction, shipyards, sanitation services, manufacturing, and domestic work.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: These industries touch the everyday lives of every Singaporean in one way or another including making sure our facilities and surroundings are properly cleaned and disinfected during this COVID-19 crisis.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Our progress these last two decades would not have been possible without their labour.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: The Marina Bay skyline, Gardens by the Bay, the Jewel and many more would not exist without our foreign workforce.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: The Building and Construction Authority or BCA reported that net operating surplus for the Construction sector alone grew by a Compounded Annual Growth Rate (CAGR) of 9.3% per annum, in nominal terms, between 2005 and 2017.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: I think it is fair to deduce that the economic contributions of our migrant workers are more than significant.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: The same can be said of our foreign domestic workers or FDWs.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: This contribution is a combination of the FDWs’ direct personal expenditure and indirectly from the real value of "paid" domestic work and value of freed-up time.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: For example, freeing mothers to participate in the labour force added S$3.5 billion to the Singapore economy.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: This includes savings of S$675 in monthly childcare costs per Singapore household.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Despite these significant contributions, our migrant workers often go unrecognised when we celebrate key milestones of Singapore’s development, be it SG50 or Bicentennial bonuses that were distributed.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: The workers are fettered to extortionate recruitment debt and most of their remaining wages go to supporting their families in their home countries.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: And the third is expenses arising from inadequate legal protection.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Many workers spend their earnings on food because their employers are not obligated to provide them with food, or fail to meet their obligations.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: MOM reported that the median monthly salary from 2005 to 2019 of work permit holders, excluding foreign domestic workers, increased by 2.2% per annum, in nominal terms.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: A 2017 TWC2 survey of 910 work permit holders employed in non-domestic sectors showed that basic salaries for first-time workers from India and Bangladesh have flat-lined since 2006 – averaging under S$600 per month.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: When adjusted for inflation, average basic salaries for first-time construction workers seem to have declined by about 20% since 2006.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: The same survey found foreign domestic workers earned an average of $597 a month in 2016.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: TWC2 informs me that Bangladeshi workers were typically paid a basic rate of $18 a day in 2004, and that rate remains unchanged to this day.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: This was largely consistent with HealthServe’s and HOME’s casework observations of Bangladeshi migrant workers, wherein $16 to $18 daily basic remains normal.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: One worker was paid a daily basic rate of $13.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: For another, his monthly salary was $158, as declared by the employer.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: To understand the extent of the stress such low wages exert on our migrant workers, we must understand where their income goes.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: This brings me to the second factor which is that a large chunk of their salary goes towards paying their recruitment debt.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: They take an average of 16.5 months to repay those fees.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: According to HOME, the entire salary of foreign domestic workers goes towards paying their recruitment fees for the first four to eight months.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Aside from debt-servicing, HealthServe informed me that the non-domestic migrant workers they serve would remit at least half of their income back home, even up to 80%.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: HOME also shared that the average foreign domestic worker remits about 80 to 90 percent of her salary.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: When a migrant worker is unpaid, underpaid, or injured, one of their major worries is how to send money back to their families.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Last but not least, after paying off a portion of their recruitment debt and remitting monies home, migrant workers must also pay for their own food, phone and transport bills out of whatever remains of their low wages.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Employers of non-domestic migrant workers are not required to bear the cost of food for their employees.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: As a result, a significant amount of migrant workers’ earnings go towards a basic necessity: food.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: I am given to understand that many dormitory dwellers do not have a say in the type of food catered, even though they have to pay for it.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Employers are required by law to ensure they have adequate food.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Yet, insufficient or poor quality food remains a top complaint among cases seen at the various migrant support centres.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: In one case that I know of, the helper was given a pack of rice containing weevils to cook and eat from!

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: If food provided to the workers cannot sustain the physical demands of their labour, we should not be surprised that our migrant workers have to purchase their own food.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Yet, like all lower income groups, migrant workers suffer from rising food prices in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Given their low wages, high debts and rising expenses, coupled with the high-risk nature of their jobs, they worry every day whether they will be able to provide for themselves and their families.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Their circumstances leave them vulnerable and deeply stressed on a daily basis – even more so in a crisis like COVID-19.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Financial support for migrant workers will go a long way in helping them manage their overwhelming financial and mental health challenges.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Without migrant workers, our buildings would not be built, our estates would not be cleaned and our women would not be able to go out and work.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Our economy blossomed on the backs of these foreign men and women.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: We cannot talk about #SGTogether or #SGUnited if we do not include and care for these 1.4 million men and women in the most tangible ways.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: This Bill is an opportunity for us to ask ourselves the kind of society we want to be.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: This COVID-19 crisis is also an opportunity for us to dip into our common humanity and ask what is Singapore in Singapore Together?

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Surely, before we extend financial assistance to individuals who do not need the relief, we should extend it to those who do in our midst?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: All three Members have spoken on different aspects of the Bill and I will seek to address their comments and feedback.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: One is permanent baseline; another is transitionary, in order to cushion the impact of the increase of the GST rate.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Earlier, I had already explained the reasons for the amendment, which is to broaden the purposes of the GST Voucher Fund, in order to enable the Assurance Package to be implemented to cushion the impact of the GST rate increase.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I also emphasised that we will continue to provide more support to lower income Singaporeans through the existing permanent GST Voucher scheme.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, the policy intent of ensuring that lower income Singaporeans get more support remains unchanged and Assoc Prof Walter Theseira can be assured that we are not moving away from this.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: In his Budget 2020 Statement, Deputy Prime Minister Heng, in fact, reiterated our public commitment for this permanent GST Voucher scheme.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: He said that it would fully offset the GST for the lower half of retiree households.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: It would significantly offset the GST for the upper half of retiree households and it would offset about half of the GST for lower income households with no elderly persons.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And as part of the review to work out the likely enhancements, we will carefully study the impact of the increased GST and the GST Voucher on Singaporeans, as Assoc Prof Theseira has suggested.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: In Budget 2020, we also made clear the Government's commitment to cushion the increase for Singaporeans as we transition to the higher GST rate.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: As our fiscal resources are limited, we will have to put Singaporeans first when we think about how to allocate these resources.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We will have to prioritise support for our citizens.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: This reflects the responsibilities and privileges of citizenship and also acknowledges our citizens' commitment to Singapore.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Ms Anthea Ong shared her concern for migrant workers who reside in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We do appreciate the contributions of migrant workers to our economy.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Many of them seek employment here to give their families back home a better life.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: While they have to pay GST, they also benefit from job opportunities here.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Rather than extend GST Vouchers to this group, we will have to look at other ways where we can address more directly the concerns and needs that migrant workers have, bearing in mind that there are also many organisations out there that play an important role in looking out for the well-being of migrant workers and ensuring that they are treated fairly and have good working conditions.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, these organisations continue to do good work and the Government will see how we can continue to work with these organisations to look out for the well-being of our migrant workers.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Ms Joan Pereira asked whether we could consider exempting GST for a list of vital healthcare items and assistive devices used by the elderly.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I will address this briefly as it does not really directly relate to the Bill.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We have a broad-based GST system with minimal exemptions and we have chosen this approach so as to keep the GST rate relatively low while we provide targeted assistance to the lower income and the elderly through subsidies and grants.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: In fact, Assoc Prof Theseira has helped to explain why we think this is a better approach and meets the objective of helping those who need help.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Today, we already absorb GST for all subsidised patients for medical services and medications in polyclinics, public hospitals or intermediate and long-term care and we will continue to do so with the GST increase.Seniors currently receive more benefits under the GST Voucher scheme through annual MediSave top-ups.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Seniors also receive significant support for their healthcare costs through other subsidies.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Seniors who need assistive devices and home care consumables can tap on the Seniors' Mobility and Enabling Fund and the Home Caregiving Grant which Ms Pereira has also highlighted.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Additional help, such as through ComCare and MediFund, would be made available to those who require further financial assistance.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Of course, seniors can also approach the agency for integrated care, for advice on the available support.
